jumped 20.7% to $133.21 in extended trading after the company announced a seven-year, $11.6 billion agreement with Anthropic.

The deal expands an existing relationship and is now the largest contract in Akamai’s history. Anthropic will use its distributed cloud infrastructure and software to support rapidly growing CPU workloads, giving Akamai a major role behind the Claude developer’s expansion.
The commitment could eventually reach $20 billion if Anthropic purchases another $9 billion of services.
Akamai’s cloud business has traditionally lived in the shadows of Amazon, Microsoft and Google. Signing one of AI’s biggest customers makes that shadow considerably smaller.
Revenue arrives later than the headline

Akamai expects no revenue from the expanded contract in 2026. It forecasts between $150 million and $300 million in the second half of 2027, followed by a gradual ramp toward an annualized run rate of around $1.7 billion by the end of 2028.

The contract uses a take-or-pay structure, meaning Anthropic must pay once Akamai delivers the agreed computing capacity. That provides greater revenue visibility than a conventional usage-based arrangement and reduces the risk of Akamai building expensive infrastructure that the customer then leaves sitting idle.

Including other cloud-infrastructure contracts signed this year, Akamai has secured roughly $14.4 billion of total committed revenue. Management expects those agreements to produce $2.2 billion in annual recurring revenue once fully operational, potentially changing the company’s overall growth profile.
Building the capacity will not be cheap

The cloud infrastructure firm expects to spend roughly $5.5 billion over the next two years to support the Anthropic commitment. That includes $1.7 billion in the fourth quarter of 2026, largely to secure memory and other critical components, followed by $3.1 billion during 2027.

A further $700 million is planned for 2028 as the final capacity comes online. Management warned that margins could face temporary pressure because data centers, equipment and power must be ready before the associated revenue reaches full speed.

Akamai estimates that its recently signed AI-cloud contracts will require between 95 and 105 megawatts of power. Once fully ramped, that infrastructure is expected to produce roughly $22 million in annual revenue per megawatt — a useful benchmark for measuring whether the buildout is earning an adequate return.
